1.title: Growth is not health
1.idea: Revenue is the money a company takes in. It says nothing about whether the company can keep going. What keeps a business alive is cash, the money it actually has. A company that spends more than it earns is burning cash, and how fast it burns is its burn rate. Divide the cash it has by its monthly burn and you get its runway: the number of months before the money runs out. When the runway ends the company has three options: borrow, sell new shares to raise cash, or close. Borrowing costs interest, and new shares make every existing owner's slice smaller. Fast growth paid for by burning cash is a bet that the company will turn profitable before the runway ends.
1.example: A company has ₹30 lakh in the bank and loses ₹3 lakh a month. Runway: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 months. Now it spends more to win customers and its loss grows to ₹5 lakh a month. Runway drops to 6 months, though it has not yet spent a rupee more from the bank. Revenue can double while the runway halves.
checks: Is the company losing money each quarter, and is the loss shrinking?
How many months of cash are left at the current burn?
Does the company explain how it reaches profit before the cash runs out?
1.rule: Revenue shows speed. Cash shows how long the journey can last.

2.title: Downloads are not customers
2.idea: Some numbers are easy to inflate: downloads, sign-ups, followers, “users”. A company can offer free trials or buy ads and watch sign-ups explode without earning a rupee. These are called vanity metrics because they look impressive and tell you little about the business. The numbers that matter turn into money: paying customers, how much each one pays, and how many keep paying. The gap between sign-ups and paying customers shows how much of the growth is real. A company whose sign-ups grow 40% a quarter while its paying customers stay flat is collecting attention, not income. Companies know which numbers look best, so the headline figure in a pitch is often the most flattering one, not the most useful.
2.example: App A has 4,00,000 sign-ups and 12,000 paying customers. App B has 20,000 sign-ups and 18,000 paying customers. App A sounds twenty times bigger. But only 3% of its sign-ups pay, against 90% for App B. If each paying customer brings ₹500 a month, App B earns ₹90 lakh and App A ₹60 lakh, even though App B is a twentieth of its size.
checks: How many customers pay, compared with the total who signed up?
Do paying customers grow as fast as sign-ups?
How much does the average paying customer bring in?
2.rule: Count the people who pay, not the people who pass by.

3.title: The leaky bucket
3.idea: A company's customer base is like a bucket filled from a tap while water leaks out of holes. New customers are the tap; customers who leave are the leaks. The share who stay from one period to the next is retention, and the share who go is churn. If the leak is large, the company must run the tap harder just to stay the same size, and winning customers is expensive: advertising, discounts, sales staff. High-retention businesses grow more cheaply because every customer they keep is one they do not have to win again. Their income also tends to be steadier, which makes them easier to understand and less likely to surprise investors.
3.example: Company X has 10,000 customers and wins 2,000 a quarter, but loses 45% of its customers each quarter (4,500). It ends at 7,500: it shrinks while looking busy. Company Y wins only 1,200 but loses 10% (1,000). It ends at 10,200, and its marketing bill is a third lower.
checks: Is retention steady or falling?
Are new customers larger than lost customers, quarter after quarter?
What does it cost to win a customer, compared with what that customer pays over time?
3.rule: Growth is new customers minus lost customers, not new customers alone.

5.title: Borrowed growth
5.idea: Borrowing lets a company grow faster than its own earnings allow, like a shopkeeper taking a loan to open a second shop. If the new shop earns more than the interest, the loan helps. If not, it hurts. The key problem is that interest is a fixed bill. It must be paid in good quarters and bad ones, and if the company cannot pay, lenders can take control. Using debt this way is called leverage: it magnifies gains in good times and losses in bad times. A useful check is interest cover, which is how many times profit before interest can pay the interest bill. Cover of 3 or more is comfortable. Cover near 1 means one weak quarter can wipe out the profit. Debt that grows faster than profit is the warning sign.
5.example: Profit before interest is ₹9 lakh a quarter and interest is ₹3 lakh, so cover is 3. Debt grows 20% a quarter for two quarters; interest rises to about ₹4.3 lakh and cover falls to about 2.1. Then one weak quarter cuts profit before interest to ₹4 lakh. Cover is now under 1, and the company makes a loss.
checks: Has debt gone up or down over the last year?
Can profit pay the interest at least three times over?
Is the income steady enough to carry the debt through a bad quarter?
5.rule: Debt is a promise to pay on a date, whether business is good or not.

7.title: Watch what insiders do
7.idea: Insiders are the people who run a company, such as the CEO and directors. They know more about it than outside investors do. When insiders buy shares with their own money, it suggests they expect the price to rise. When they sell, the reason may be harmless: paying for a home, covering taxes, spreading their own risk. But a pattern of heavy, repeated selling, especially while the company tells everyone how well it is doing, is a warning to look harder. Actions with your own money carry more information than words in a press release. So compare what leaders say with what they do.
7.example: A CEO who owns 1,00,000 shares and sells 5,000 once in a year is probably doing something ordinary. A CEO who sells 30,000 across three quarters in a row while describing “record growth” is a signal to check the company's cash, customers and debt.
checks: Is this one sale or a pattern across quarters?
What share of the insider's holding is being sold?
Do other signals, like cash and customers, agree or disagree?
7.rule: Listen to what insiders say, but watch what they do with their own money.

10.title: Time does the heavy lifting
10.idea: Compounding means your gains earn gains of their own. If an investment grows 10% in a year, next year's 10% applies to the larger amount. The effect is small at first and then speeds up, which is why time does more work than almost anything else. Selling a sound business early gives up this later growth, and costs fees on the way out and again when you reinvest. This does not mean never sell. It means sell for a reason in the data: the business weakened, or you need the money. A small gain is not a reason by itself, and neither is a price that moved a little.
10.example: ₹50,000 growing 10% a year becomes about ₹1,29,700 after 10 years, a gain of ₹79,700. After 20 years it is about ₹3,36,400. The second ten years added about ₹2,06,700, more than twice what the first ten added, at the same rate.
checks: Has anything about the business worsened, or only the price?
Am I selling because of data, or because I feel uneasy?
What will this sale and the next purchase cost in fees?
10.rule: Sell on bad data, not on a small gain.

11.title: A falling price is not a falling business
11.terms: Volatility, market risk versus company risk
11.idea: Prices move for two kinds of reasons. Some are about the company: lost customers, rising debt, falling profit. Others are about the whole market: fear, news, a slowdown. In a broad fall even strong companies drop, because many investors sell everything at once. Many recover when confidence returns, though not all and not on any schedule. Volatility is how much and how fast prices move; it is normal, and it is part of owning something that can grow. The skill is telling the two kinds of reasons apart. If the business data is unchanged, the fall is mostly noise. If the data is getting worse, the fall may be telling you something real.
11.example: Your company's price falls 20% in a quarter, from ₹100 to ₹80. Its profit is unchanged, customers are up 1%, and it holds more cash than debt. If it later returns to ₹100, that is a 25% gain from ₹80. Selling at ₹80 locks in a loss the business never actually earned.
checks: Did customers, margin or cash change, or only the price?
How did similar companies move at the same time?
Do I need this money soon? (See “Money you'll need soon”.)
11.rule: Ask whether the business changed, not just whether the price did.

14.title: Rumours and “guaranteed”
14.terms: Information quality, unverified news, investment fraud
14.idea: Reliable information can be checked: reported numbers, official filings, news from several trusted sources, or answers a company gives you with figures. Rumours, tips from friends and posts from strangers cannot be checked, and the person passing them on often gains if you believe them. Pushing up a price so insiders can sell at a high is an old trick. A promise of guaranteed returns is the clearest red flag of all: every real investment can lose money, and anyone who will not admit that is either mistaken or dishonest. This connects directly to scam awareness, because the same tactics of urgency, secrecy and special access appear in investment frauds.
14.example: A message says: “Put in ₹10,000 this week. Guaranteed ₹20,000 in three months. Only 20 places left.” Doubling in three months, repeated four times, would turn ₹10,000 into ₹1,60,000 in a year. No real business can promise that. The “20 places left” line is there to make you decide before you check.
checks: Who is telling me this, and what do they gain if I believe it?
Can I confirm the claim from the company's own numbers?
Is there pressure to act fast or to keep it secret?
14.rule: If someone guarantees a return, walk away.

16.title: Too many eggs in one basket
16.idea: Diversification means spreading your money across different things so that no single problem can sink you. The key word is different. Companies in the same sector often fall together when that sector gets bad news, so owning several of them is closer to one big bet than to several small ones. Companies in unrelated sectors face different risks, so a bad stretch for one is often balanced by a steadier one elsewhere. Diversification does not remove risk and it does not guarantee a profit. It lowers the chance that one surprise decides your whole result, and it usually smooths the ride. It also has a price: you give up the chance of putting everything on the single best performer.
16.example: Portfolio A holds ₹90,000 in one sector and ₹10,000 elsewhere. That sector falls 30%: the loss is ₹27,000, or 27% of the total. Portfolio B holds ₹30,000 in each of three unrelated sectors. The same sector falls 30%: the loss is ₹9,000, or 9%. Same shock, one third of the damage.
checks: How many truly different sectors do my holdings cover?
Would my holdings react to the same bad news?
Is any one holding big enough to decide my result?
16.rule: Spread across different risks, not just different names.

20.title: Every trade has a cost
20.idea: Every purchase and sale has a cost: fees, and the gap between buying and selling prices. The costs look small, but they come out of your money every time, and they compound against you just as returns compound for you. Frequent trading also makes it more likely that you act on feelings rather than information: a scary headline, a tip, a bad day. Studies of real investors have found that those who trade most often tend to do worse, largely because of costs and poor timing. This does not mean never trade. It means each trade should have a reason you could write in one sentence, based on data you did not have a month ago.
20.example: With a 1% fee on each buy and each sale, one round trip costs about 2%. If you make 10 round trips in a year, you need roughly 20% of gains just to cover the fees before earning anything. Buying once and holding costs 2% once.
checks: What new data led to this trade?
What will this trade cost me in total?
Would I still make it if I had to explain my reason in one sentence?

21.title: Idle money loses value
21.idea: Inflation means prices rise over time, so each rupee buys a little less each year. Money sitting idle keeps its number but loses buying power. Cash has an important job: it pays for what you need soon and it protects you from having to sell investments at a bad time. But holding far more than that, for years, has a cost too: you give up what the money might have earned elsewhere. This is called opportunity cost. The aim is not to invest everything. It is to give each part of your money a job and a timeline: cash for what you need soon, and investments for what can wait.
21.example: ₹1,00,000 in cash with prices rising 5% a year buys what ₹95,000 buys today after one year, and about what ₹78,000 buys today after five years. The number stays the same, but its buying power shrinks by more than a fifth.
checks: What is this money for, and when will I need it?
How much cash do I truly need for emergencies?
Is the rest waiting for a reason, or just for courage?
21.rule: Waiting is a choice with a cost.

22.title: Money you'll need soon
22.idea: Liquidity is how quickly and cheaply you can turn something into cash without losing value. The prices of investments go up and down, so if you need money on a particular date, you may be forced to sell at a bad moment. That is why money you will need within a year or two should not sit in risky investments. An emergency fund is a cushion kept in a safe, easy-to-reach form, big enough to cover several months of expenses. It protects your investments as much as it protects you: with a cushion, a market fall is something you can wait out instead of something you are forced to sell into. The idea is to match each pot of money to its timeline, with near-term needs in safe places and long-term goals in investments that can ride out the swings.
22.example: You need ₹25,000 and hold ₹10,000 in cash plus a company you bought at ₹100 that is now at ₹70. You sell ₹15,000 worth at the low price, locking in a 30% loss. With a ₹25,000 cushion you would not have sold at all, and if the price later returned to ₹100 you would have kept the whole recovery.
checks: When will I need this money?
What would I do if I needed it next month?
Do I have a cushion that does not depend on selling?
22.rule: Money you need soon belongs somewhere safe.
